reports.sample: 2,780 ledger rows across the .tofu/log day files, of which 1,458 are tool_gate, 1,105 stop_check and 13 shell_sift, with 204 ad hoc judge questions excluded as not a threshold point
reports.skips: the 204 inline rows are excluded with the reason stated; ask is counted as zero rows because no writer exists for it, which the report distinguishes from having no labels

conclusion.text: Hand read from bench/report/handread.json: The ledger holds 2,780 decision rows and 20 of them carry an outcome, all hand labelled and all attached to tool_gate. Exactly one labelled row sits near a threshold, within three dead bands of risk_deny_at, and none sits near risk_ask_at; stop_check and shell_sift have none at all. A threshold needs roughly 60 labels near its operating point at a 5 percent false positive budget and 300 at 1 percent, so no point is calibratable at either and tool_gate alone needs 59 more near one threshold and 60 near the other. The reach of three dead bands is argued rather than assumed: one dead band is the tie zone the decision code already uses, so a label sitting inside it proves nothing about where the line should sit. There is no arrival rate, because all 20 outcomes were written in a 78 second window five days ago and nothing since, with nineteen of them inside two seconds, which the report calls consistent with a scripted loop rather than a person. Its conclusion is that hand labelling cannot close the gap and the shadow gate writing outcomes automatically is the path that scales. It also found that the ask point has never written a ledger row at all, which is a missing writer rather than a labelling gap.

reports.sample: one recorded 11 step turn measured in full, plus 51 of 111 recorded turns carrying cache accounting, of which 24 wrote to cache and 15 are at today's 18 tool scale
reports.skips: 60 of 111 turns carry no usable cache accounting, either predating it or holding no steps, and the report gives the split. No live model call was made and no account was spent.

conclusion.text: Hand read from bench/report/handread.json: The tool schemas a turn sends cost 16,575 bytes on every request, about 4,143 tokens for all 18 tools, and deferring them is not worth building. The figure is measured by encoding a real request with and without the tools array and taking the difference; summing the tools individually gives 16,492, and the 83 byte gap is the array's own brackets and commas. Caching is what decides it: on the measured turn the block was written to cache once on step one and never again across eleven steps, and 81.6 percent of that turn's billed input was cache reads. Across the corpus, 24 recorded turns wrote to cache and 23 of them made a second model call and read the write back; at today's 18 tool scale, 14 of 15 did. The deferral mechanism is named and costed rather than assumed: a catalog line plus a fetch before first use would have added 5 round trips to the measured turn to save at most 2,873 tokens, paid once at cache-write price. The only case it would pay is a turn that makes exactly one model call and never returns, which was 1 of 24.

reports.state_note: the cohort section only, withdrawn on 2026-09-23 by TOFU-529 and by this file rather than by an edit to the report. The reader that produced those counts tagged its fields with the older capitalized spellings only, so it decoded 51 of the 58 single file sessions to all zero and classified each of them as predating cache accounting. The shared reader handles both spellings, and on the same corpus the usable turns rise from 51 to 97 and the turns carrying a cache write from 24 to 38. Every count, dollar and percentage in that section was computed over a sample less than half the size it should have been, so the figures fall. The verdict does not: the schema block is still written to cache once and read back on every later step, and the corrected sample makes that stronger rather than weaker. The headline figure of 16,575 bytes and 4,143 tokens is measured from the wire encoder rather than the corpus and stands unchanged, as does the single turn measured in full.

conclusion.text: Hand read from bench/report/handread.json: Five independent readers of the recorded sessions exist where one shared reader is imported by nineteen packages, and three of the four extras have a real reason: one needs per step token fields the shared record does not carry, one needs occupancy and fork and compaction and reads through the session store instead, and one is a byte scan for a quota key rather than a turn parse. Only one re-walks by hand what the shared walker already does, and that is a clean merge. The most repeated shape is the smallest: six separate declarations of a skip record holding a path and a reason, with two pairs sharing a name across different packages. Two apparent duplications are left alone with arguments: a nearest rank percentile over integers is correct where an interpolated float one is not, because a fractional value between two byte counts means nothing. One thing that looks like duplication is named as not being any: four packages sum a cost with the same loop, and each sums a different field on a different struct answering a different question, so a shared helper would save one line per site and put a layer between the reader and the field. Nothing was merged, deleted or rewritten: the deliverable is the list and the judgment.

This one reaches the results over it, where the arm genuinely cuts, and the judged cut removes a further 3,367 of 24,619 tokens, 13.7 percent, against the 1.5 percent mechanical floor from TOFU-338. Nine distinct over-cap read and search artifacts were identified in the corpus and 3 were judged inside a stated cap of 250 live calls; 247 calls were made for $0.013247, against 393 calls and $0.040968 for the first run. The worked example is a design document, not a test log: fixed truncation drops 781 bytes from its middle and every one of those bytes falls inside a single paragraph the judgment marked keep, so truncation by position drops exactly the part the judgment says still matters. The 6 unjudged artifacts are each skipped with a named reason, a paragraph count over the remaining call budget, and two of them are 798 paragraph reads that would need roughly 0.18 dollars more to judge.

The arm it is compared against did not fire on this sample: all 8 measured results are under the 32,768 byte truncation cap and the largest is 12,793 bytes, so the 1.9 percent came off results fixed truncation would have passed through whole. 9 of 39 stored read and search artifacts in the corpus exceed the cap and none fell inside the live call budget, so the arm-firing comparison cannot be made on this sample.
